name: Garhwal
tagline: Four dhams, two rivers, one long climb
meta_description: Plan Garhwal, Uttarakhand: Char Dham, Valley of Flowers, Rishikesh, Mussoorie and Auli, with honest bus fares, GMVN stays and trips from saver to signature.
summary: Garhwal is the western half of Uttarakhand, where the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rise and join to become the Ganga. Come for the Char Dham shrines, Valley of Flowers, Tungnath and Rishikesh. Go May–June or mid-September–October; avoid July road travel. A saver week by UTC bus and GMVN dorms costs about ₹2,000–3,000 a day.
intro: Garhwal runs from the Doon Valley and Rishikesh at 340 m to the Tibet border above Mana and Nelang. It is seven districts: Dehradun, Haridwar, Tehri, Pauri, Uttarkashi, Rudraprayag and Chamoli. The name comes from garh, a fort: medieval Garhwal was a patchwork of hill forts until the Panwar kings joined them into one kingdom. Kumaon, the eastern half of Uttarakhand, is a separate hive with its own language, food and history, and we plan it separately.

Most visitors come for faith. The four shrines of the Char Dham, Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath, sit at 3,100–3,600 m at the heads of four river valleys and open only from late April to November. In season the yatra roads carry lakhs of pilgrims, and the whole economy of the high valleys, from pony handlers to dhaba cooks, turns on those six months.

Between the shrines are the places that need no temple to justify a trip: the Valley of Flowers in July and August, the walk from Chopta to Tungnath and Chandrashila, the apple orchards of Harsil, the ski slopes of Auli in January, and the old cantonment lanes of Landour above Mussoorie. Rishikesh, at the bottom of it all, is where the Ganga leaves the hills and where most journeys begin.

We plan Garhwal at three prices. Saver trips use UTC and GMOU buses from Rishikesh, shared jeeps, GMVN rest houses, dharamshalas and Zostel. Comfort trips use a private car with driver and the best hotels each town has, which in the high valleys means clean and warm rather than plush. Signature trips pair Ananda, Taj Rishikesh and JW Marriott Mussoorie with a private guide and helicopter seats to Kedarnath where they make sense.

story.title: Garhwal: forts, rivers and the yatra road

chapters.heading: A kingdom of fifty-two forts
chapters.text: Garhwal means the country of forts. Local tradition counts fifty-two small chiefdoms, each with its own garh, before the Panwar dynasty, whose story begins at Chandpur Garhi and whose capital moved to Devalgarh and then Srinagar on the Alaknanda, brought them under one crown. In 1803 the Gorkha army of Nepal took the kingdom, and their general Amar Singh Thapa is credited with building the first Gangotri temple during the occupation. After the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–16 the British kept eastern Garhwal, with Kedarnath and Badrinath, and returned the west to the Panwar king Sudarshan Shah, who built a new capital at Tehri. That split explains why old records speak of British Garhwal and Tehri Garhwal, and why the royal family of Tehri still announces the Badrinath opening date each spring.

chapters.heading: The pilgrim road and its chattis
chapters.text: For centuries pilgrims walked to the four dhams from Haridwar and Rishikesh, a round trip of weeks. They slept at chattis, simple halts a day's walk apart, and some names on today's road maps still carry the word, such as Janki Chatti and Hanuman Chatti below Yamunotri. Income from villages along the route once fed and sheltered pilgrims at Badrinath. Motor roads reached the shrines only in the twentieth century. The chattis survive as dhabas, and the ponies, palkis and kandis at Gaurikund and Janki Chatti are the last working part of that walking economy.

chapters.heading: Women who hugged the trees
chapters.text: In March 1974, in Reni village above the Rishiganga near Joshimath, contractors arrived to fell 2,500 trees while the village men had been called away to Chamoli. Gaura Devi, head of the village women's group, led 27 women into the forest. They put their arms around the trees and kept watch through the night until the loggers left. The action grew out of a protest begun in April 1973 at Mandal near Gopeshwar, organised by Chandi Prasad Bhatt's Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh. It became known as Chipko, from the Hindi for to cling, and it changed forest policy across India. When you drive the Niti valley road beyond Joshimath, you pass the same slopes.

chapters.heading: Floods, rebuilding and a new caution
chapters.text: Garhwal's rivers are young and steep, and the valleys have paid for it. On 16 and 17 June 2013 water and debris from Chorabari Tal swept through Kedarnath; thousands of pilgrims and residents died along the Mandakini. The temple itself stood, shielded by a large rock that lodged behind it, now worshipped as Bhim Shila. In February 2021 a rock and ice avalanche sent a flood down the Rishiganga past Reni, and in January 2023 Joshimath's slow subsidence became a crisis. In August 2025 a flash flood struck Dharali near Harsil. Each event changed the rules: mandatory registration, weather holds and daily caps. We plan around them with spare days and honest advice.

Free Char Dham registration; Gangotri NP and Valley of Flowers entry permits
Mana village road above Badrinath, ≈ 3,200 m
Jio and Airtel on yatra towns; patchy on treks and passes

highlights.title: The Char Dham circuit
highlights.text: Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath in one 10–11 night loop from Rishikesh. Two of the four need a walk: 6 km to Yamunotri from Janki Chatti and about 16–17 km to Kedarnath from Gaurikund. Registration is free and mandatory; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Valley of Flowers in monsoon
highlights.text: A UNESCO-listed hanging valley at 3,350–3,650 m, open June to October and at its fullest from mid-July to late August. You sleep at Ghangaria, walk in for the day and leave by 5 pm. Pair it with the 6 km climb to Hemkund Sahib.

highlights.title: Tungnath and Chandrashila
highlights.text: The highest of the five Panch Kedar temples, at 3,680 m, is a 3.5 km paved climb from Chopta. Another 1.5 km of steep path takes you to Chandrashila, over 4,000 m, for a view that runs from Bandarpunch to Nanda Devi. It works in every season except deep monsoon.

highlights.title: Rishikesh mornings
highlights.text: Yoga at 6 am, a walk across Ram Jhula, Ganga aarti at Triveni Ghat or Parmarth Niketan at dusk, and from mid-September to June, rafting from Shivpuri. The city is vegetarian and alcohol-free by law, which keeps the riverfront quiet after dark.

highlights.title: Harsil apples and the Bhagirathi
highlights.text: A wide valley of deodar and orchards at 2,745 m on the Gangotri road. Apples, introduced here in the nineteenth century by the English deserter Frederick Wilson, ripen in September and October, and the winter seat of the goddess Ganga sits across the river at Mukhba.

highlights.title: Auli in snow
highlights.text: India's best-known ski slope sits at about 2,800 m above Joshimath, with a chairlift, GMVN ski courses of 7 and 14 days, and Nanda Devi straight ahead. January to early March brings reliable snow; the rest of the year it is a meadow walk with the same view.

budget.covers: GMVN dorm or dharamshala bed, dhaba thalis, UTC/GMOU bus and shared jeep seats
Private car with driver (shared by two), 3-star hotel or good homestay, all meals
Ananda, Taj or JW Marriott nights, private guide, car and helicopter seats where used

money_savers: Take the 5 am UTC or GMOU buses from Rishikesh ISBT or the GMOU yard instead of a private taxi; Rishikesh to Sonprayag costs ₹500–800 a seat against ₹7,000–9,000 for a car.
Book GMVN rest house dorms at Badrinath, Ghangaria, Gangotri and Uttarkashi as soon as yatra dates are fixed; they fill fast in May and June.
Travel in the second half of September or October, when hotel rates on the yatra road drop by a third or more after the monsoon.
Walk to Kedarnath if you are fit and acclimatised; a return pony costs several thousand rupees and a helicopter seat ₹6,000–13,000 return.
Eat thalis at gurdwaras and dhabas; the langar at Govindghat and Ghangaria gurdwaras is free and open to all.
Draw cash in Rishikesh, Srinagar, Uttarkashi or Joshimath; ATMs above these towns run dry in peak weeks and many dhabas take only cash or UPI with weak signal.
getting_there: Most journeys start in Rishikesh or Haridwar. Delhi to Haridwar is about 4.5 hours by Shatabdi or Vande Bharat train, and Yog Nagari Rishikesh station takes some through trains. Dehradun's Jolly Grant airport, with flights from Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other cities, is about 35 km from Rishikesh. Overnight Volvo and Uttarakhand Transport Corporation buses run from Delhi ISBT Kashmere Gate to Rishikesh and Dehradun in 6–7 hours. From Rishikesh, UTC buses and the private Garhwal Motor Owners' Union buses leave between 4 am and 7 am for Uttarkashi, Barkot, Sonprayag, Ukhimath, Joshimath and Badrinath. The Rishikesh–Karnaprayag railway is under construction and not yet open for passengers; check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian and foreign pilgrims must register for the Char Dham and Hemkund Sahib on the Uttarakhand Tourism Development Board's registration portal or app before travelling; counters in Rishikesh and Haridwar handle walk-ins. Registration is free and is checked on the road. Valley of Flowers and Gangotri National Park (Gaumukh) need forest entry permits, and Gaumukh has a daily cap. Nelang valley beyond Harsil is an inner-line area with its own permit. Rules change every season; check current status before you travel.

months.summary: The four dhams are shut and their deities sit in winter seats at Kharsali, Mukhba, Ukhimath and Joshimath. This is ski month at Auli, and Chopta often lies under snow, which turns the Tungnath walk into a winter trek. Rishikesh and Mussoorie are cold, clear and quiet, with low hotel prices outside New Year week. Roads to Joshimath and Ukhimath stay open but black ice is common at dawn.
months.tip: Book GMVN ski courses at Auli early, as the January batches fill first.

months.summary: Snow still covers Auli and the upper Chopta road, and the ski season peaks in the first half of the month. Lower down, Rishikesh warms up and the yoga schools run full timetables. Mussoorie and Landour can get a fresh snowfall, which brings Delhi weekend crowds for a day or two. On Basant Panchami the date for opening Badrinath is announced at the Tehri royal palace in Narendra Nagar.
months.tip: Carry microspikes for Tungnath if you go after a fresh fall.

months.summary: A fine month for the lower half of Garhwal. Rishikesh hosts the International Yoga Festival in the first week, rafting runs on clear green water, and rhododendrons begin to flower on the Chopta and Mussoorie ridges. Snow lingers on Chandrashila, so the summit is a proper winter climb. The Char Dham roads are being cleared, and registration for the yatra usually opens online this month.
months.tip: Register for the Char Dham online as soon as the portal opens if you want early-May dates.

months.summary: Buransh turns the forests red around Chopta and Deoria Tal, and Mussoorie fills with families escaping the plains. In the second half of the month the yatra begins: Yamunotri and Gangotri open on Akshaya Tritiya, and Kedarnath and Badrinath follow within days. The first week of the yatra is very crowded and hotels at Guptkashi and Badrinath are at their highest rates.
months.tip: Avoid the opening week itself unless the ceremony is your reason for going.

months.summary: Peak yatra month. All four shrines are open, Hemkund Sahib opens late in the month, and snow walls still line parts of the Kedarnath path. Kafal fruit is on sale along the roads. The plains heat pushes crowds to Mussoorie and the dhams, so roads jam at Sonprayag and Badrinath and car parks fill by 8 am. Rishikesh is hot but the river is cold and rafting is in full swing.
months.tip: Start every yatra drive before 6 am to beat the queues at checkposts.

months.summary: The Valley of Flowers opens on 1 June with early primulas and snow bridges, and the yatra stays busy until monsoon rain arrives, usually in the last third of the month. Ganga Dussehra falls in May or June and brings crowds to the Rishikesh ghats. From late June, landslides begin to close the highways for hours at a time; build spare days into any plan.
months.tip: Finish high-altitude treks by mid-June if you want dry trails.

months.summary: Monsoon month. The Valley of Flowers comes into bloom, but the roads to it, and to Kedarnath and Gangotri, suffer frequent landslides, and the government may pause the yatra on red-alert days. Rafting in Rishikesh is closed. If you must travel, choose the Valley of Flowers with two buffer days and travel insurance, and watch district weather alerts every evening.
months.tip: Check IMD and district alerts each night and never drive the hill roads after dark in rain.

months.summary: The best flower weeks in the Valley of Flowers fall between late July and late August, with blue poppies, balsam and brahma kamal at Hemkund. Rain continues and road closures still happen, so this is a month for patient travellers. Mussoorie is green and misty. Hotel rates along the yatra road are at their lowest of the open season.
months.tip: Keep two spare days between Ghangaria and your train or flight home.

months.summary: The monsoon eases by mid-month and the views return, washed and sharp. Pilgrim numbers rise again for the second yatra season, but crowds are thinner than in May. Harsil's apple harvest begins, the Valley of Flowers still holds late blooms, and rafting usually resumes around mid-September once the river drops. Early September can still bring heavy rain.
months.tip: Plan high trips from the 15th onward and keep the first half for Rishikesh and Mussoorie.

months.summary: Our favourite month. Clear skies, cold nights, golden grass on the bugyals and the best mountain views of the year from Chandrashila, Auli and Badrinath. The yatra is steady but calm, and hotels offer post-monsoon rates. Gangotri, Kedarnath and Yamunotri close around Diwali, which falls in October or November, so check the closing dates before you plan.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket; nights at Kedarnath and Badrinath go below freezing.

months.summary: The dhams close one by one, Badrinath last, usually in mid-to-late November. Doli processions carry the deities down to their winter seats, and the high villages of Mana and Ghangaria empty for winter. Rishikesh and Mussoorie are pleasant and uncrowded, and Chopta is cold and clear. A quiet month for travellers who want views without queues.
months.tip: Join a doli procession at Ukhimath or Mukhba if your dates match.

months.summary: Cold, dry and clear, with the first snow at Auli and Chopta late in the month. Mussoorie and Landour fill for Christmas and New Year, when hotel prices spike for a week. Rishikesh is calm, with cool sunny afternoons on the ghats. Winter-seat temples at Ukhimath and Joshimath see a steady trickle of pilgrims who cannot wait for spring.
months.tip: Book Mussoorie for 24 December to 1 January at least six weeks ahead.

faqs.q: How much does a Char Dham Yatra cost on a budget?
faqs.a: A saver Char Dham of 10–11 nights by UTC and GMOU bus, shared jeep and GMVN dorms or dharamshalas costs about ₹18,000–28,000 per person from Rishikesh, including simple meals. Ponies, palkis and helicopter seats are extra and can double that. A private car with 3-star hotels costs ₹55,000–75,000 per person for two sharing. Prices are indicative for 2026.

faqs.q: Is registration mandatory for the Char Dham Yatra?
faqs.a: Yes. Every pilgrim must register on the Uttarakhand Tourism Development Board portal or app, or at offline counters in Rishikesh and Haridwar. Registration is free, needs an ID such as Aadhaar or a passport, and gives you a dated slip or QR code that police check on the road. Hemkund Sahib needs registration too. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When do the Char Dham temples open and close?
faqs.a: Yamunotri and Gangotri open on Akshaya Tritiya, usually late April or early May, and Kedarnath and Badrinath open within days. Gangotri closes on Govardhan Puja after Diwali, Kedarnath and Yamunotri on Bhai Dooj, and Badrinath in mid-to-late November. Dates are announced each year by the temple committees; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Garhwal?
faqs.a: For the dhams and treks, May to mid-June and mid-September to October. For the Valley of Flowers, mid-July to late August, accepting rain. For snow and skiing at Auli, January to early March. Rishikesh works all year except the sticky months of May and June, and rafting closes from July to mid-September.

faqs.q: Is Garhwal safe during the monsoon?
faqs.a: The people are safe; the roads are the risk. From late June to mid-September, landslides close highways for hours or days, and the state can halt the yatra on heavy-rain alerts. If you travel then, keep two buffer days, avoid driving after dark, take insurance, and follow district alerts. Never camp near riverbeds or streams in rain.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness at Kedarnath or Badrinath?
faqs.a: It is possible. Kedarnath is 3,583 m and Hemkund about 4,600 m, and many pilgrims climb straight from the plains. Sleep a night at Guptkashi or Joshimath first, walk slowly, drink water and avoid alcohol. Headache with vomiting or breathlessness at rest means go down. Talk to your doctor before the trip, especially if you have heart or lung conditions.

faqs.q: Is mobile network and ATM access available on the yatra?
faqs.a: Jio and Airtel work in most yatra towns, including Kedarnath, Badrinath and Gangotri, but drop out in gorges and on treks such as Ghangaria to the Valley of Flowers. ATMs exist in Rishikesh, Srinagar, Rudraprayag, Uttarkashi, Guptkashi and Joshimath; carry enough cash for 3–4 days above these towns.

faqs.q: Is Garhwal suitable for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, with ordinary care. Rishikesh, Mussoorie and the yatra towns are used to solo women, and the Char Dham roads are busy with families. Stay in GMVN rest houses, Zostel or well-reviewed hotels, travel by day, and share your plan with someone at home. On remote treks such as Gaumukh, a registered guide is mandatory anyway.

faqs.q: Can seniors and children do the Char Dham?
faqs.a: Many do. Badrinath and Gangotri are a short walk from the car park. Yamunotri (6 km) and Kedarnath (about 16–17 km) need a walk, pony, palki or, for Kedarnath, a helicopter seat. Seniors should get a medical check, sleep lower the night before, and avoid the first week of the yatra. Children under five feel the cold badly at Kedarnath.
